::: {.callout-tip}
## One coherent example

We use six invented shop orders with **distance (km)**, **number of items**, and **fulfilment time (minutes)**. Start the [single-file Python example](../../examples/README.md); this chapter corresponds to `python3 delivery_ml_lab.py calculus`.
:::

## The motivating problem

**What changes in a model when its parameters change?**

Derivatives and gradients are local sensitivity measures. Jacobians handle vector-valued functions; the chain rule leads to backpropagation; Hessians and Taylor expansions describe curvature. Learning these relationships explains optimisation beyond calling an API.

## Central mathematical relationship

$$
L(\beta)=\frac1N\|X\beta-y\|_2^2,\qquad \nabla L(\beta)=\frac2N X^\top(X\beta-y)
$$

The equation captures the chapter's principal relationship. Definitions and assumptions are developed in the lessons below; an equation is useful only when the domain and meaning of its symbols are explicit.

## First worked result

If one order has feature row (1,2,1), measured time 9, and current beta=(3,2,1), then prediction is 8 and the gradient of squared loss is (-2,-4,-2). This gives a concrete local update direction.

## What to pay attention to

A gradient gives a local direction but not a guaranteed global minimum on nonconvex losses. Every derivative rule needs domain and differentiability assumptions.

Read the lessons in sequence, reproduce a calculation by hand, then run the related Python demonstration and explain which mathematical claim the output illustrates. A numerical observation is never, by itself, proof of a theorem.
